contexts.text: They could never put on another countenance, except according to what they were thinking. AC 4326:3. SE 3317.
(From the countenance the character is known.) AC 6616.
Hence man is sometimes affected by the countenance of another, although this is not from his countenance, but from the mind thus shining forth.
As the natural mind represents itself in the face and its expression... for as the face is the countenance of the natural mind, so the natural mind ought to be the countenance of the rational mind.
Hence the face or countenance = the states of the thoughts and the states of the affections.

Man's face, by its various expressions, represents both his thought and his will. Everybody knows that the face represents through its expressions; for from the expressions of the face with the sincere, may be seen their interior states.
The deceitful put on a most friendly expression. SE 2856.
By the formations of the countenance...
The affections are manifested through the expressions, and their changes...
No one there can hide his interiors by his expression. HH 457:end.
From infancy men learn to induce expressions on their faces...

The variations of the face, which are called the expressions, correspond to the affections of the disposition: wherefore the face is varied as to its expressions, as are the affections of the disposition as to their states.
